summary.text: Take \(n=0\). Since \(\Phi_1(0)=-1\) and every \(\Phi_k\) with \(k>1\) has constant term \(1\), the absolute value of \(\Phi_k(0)\) is always \(1\), hence never prime.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\Phi_k(x)\in\mathbb Z[x]\) denote the \(k\)-th cyclotomic polynomial. The statement actually proved false is
\[
 \forall n\in\mathbb N\;\exists k\in\mathbb N,
 \qquad k>0\quad\text{and}\quad |\Phi_k(n)|\text{ is prime}.
\]
Here the absolute value is present because \(\Phi_k(n)\) is an integer, whereas primality is being asserted of a nonnegative integer.

We use \(n=0\) as a counterexample. The relevant values of the cyclotomic polynomials at zero are
\[
 \Phi_1(0)=-1
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \Phi_k(0)=1\quad\text{for every }k>1.
\]
For completeness, these facts follow directly from the standard cyclotomic factorization. First,
\[
 \Phi_1(x)=x-1,
\]
so \(\Phi_1(0)=-1\).

We now prove that \(\Phi_k(0)=1\) for every integer \(k>1\). Recall that for every positive integer \(m\),
\[
 x^m-1=\prod_{d\mid m}\Phi_d(x).
\]
We argue by strong induction on \(m>1\). On substituting \(x=0\) into this factorization, we obtain
\[
 -1=\prod_{d\mid m}\Phi_d(0).
\]
Among the divisors of \(m\) are \(1\) and \(m\). Every other divisor \(d\) satisfies \(1<d<m\), and hence, by the strong induction hypothesis, \(\Phi_d(0)=1\). Since \(\Phi_1(0)=-1\), the displayed product therefore reduces to
\[
 -1=\Phi_1(0)\,\Phi_m(0)
    =-\Phi_m(0).
\]
Thus \(\Phi_m(0)=1\). This also supplies the base case automatically: when \(m=2\), there are no divisors strictly between \(1\) and \(2\), so the same calculation gives \(-1=(-1)\Phi_2(0)\). The induction proves the claimed constant-term formula for every \(m>1\).

Now suppose, toward the asserted universal statement, that there were some positive index \(k\) for which \(|\Phi_k(0)|\) were prime. Because \(k>0\), there are exactly two cases.

1. If \(k=1\), then
\[
 |\Phi_k(0)|=|\Phi_1(0)|=|-1|=1.
\]
But \(1\) is not prime.

2. If \(k\ne 1\), positivity of \(k\) implies \(k>1\). By the constant-term result just proved,
\[
 |\Phi_k(0)|=|1|=1,
\]
which again is not prime.

Thus no positive integer \(k\) makes \(|\Phi_k(0)|\) prime. Equivalently, the set
\[
 \{k>0:|\Phi_k(0)|\text{ is prime}\}
\]
is empty, so there is no least such \(k\), and \(a(0)\) is not defined in the intended “least successful index” sense. Consequently the universal assertion over all natural numbers \(n\), when \(0\in\mathbb N\), is false.

There is an essential domain qualification. The counterexample is \(n=0\). Therefore this argument disproves the formal statement quantified over every natural number, including zero. It does not disprove the literally stated conjecture “for every positive integer \(n\)” if “positive” is understood as \(n\ge 1\), as is also suggested by the OEIS sequence’s offset \(1\). Under that strictly positive-domain reading, \(0\) is outside the domain and the accepted argument gives no counterexample.
